PROPOSED INCREASE IN PRICE OF OIL AND GAS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Whereas the government seems to plan an incredible increase of more than 30 per cent in the price of oil, and whereas such a step would mean an increase of at least 30 cents to 45 cents per gallon of gas and 20 cents to 30 cents per gallon of heating oil, and whereas such an increase would mean an additional cost of at least $140 per year per car driver, and at least $160 per year per household, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Lalonde):
That this House directs the government not to make any change to the present arrangements that provide for an increase of only three cents to four cents per gallon of gas between now and June 30, 1980.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY CONCERNING UNJUST DISMISSALS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the terms of Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House.
Considering that in recent months thousands of civil servants with 15 to 25 years of seniority in the civil service were fired with no other explanation than the fact that their numbers had to be reduced, and considering that recent medical
reports have since raised the spectre of infarct, coronary thrombosis, alcoholism and depression apparently settling in at an alarming rate because these unjust and inhuman methods have been resorted to, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle (Mr. Lefebvre):
That this House condem the use of such methods and that an order be given for an inquiry to be instituted in the matter of firings in the civil service which, to all practical purposes, are now discriminatory and contrary to the most elementary justice.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT IJC STUDY HARMFUL EFFECTS OF RADIATION LEAKAGES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Because a 1,280 megawatt boiling water nuclear power installation is proposed for Sedro Woolley, Washington, a site contiguous to the Canada-U.S. border, and should construction proceed any future accident would threaten the lives of almost one million people in B.C.'s lower mainland, I move, seconded by the hon. member for New Westminster-Coquit-lam (Miss Jewett):
That (1) Canada issue to the United States an aide memoire calling for a moratorium on the Sedro Woolley plant with a view to its relocation away from Canadian population centres;
(2) that during President Carter's visit here our Prime Minister discuss the concern of many Canadians over nuclear installations and the lethal effects of radiation leakage, and depending on the outcome of discussions between the two leaders, Canada consider initiating a reference to the International Joint Commission for study and recommendations.

EFFECT ON MANITOBA WATER SYSTEMS-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a motion of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that there is increasing uncertainty over the American government's intentions in relation to the Garrison irrigation project in North Dakota, in view of the fact that any form of biological linkage between the Garrison water systems and Manitoba would result in substantial environmental damage and seriously harm the fishing industry in Manitoba, and in view of the impending visit of President Carter to Canada on November 9, I move, seconded by the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Bockstael):
That the matter of the Garrison irrigation project be placed on the agenda for discussion as a priority issue and that the Canadian government convey to the President that there should be no form of linkage between the Garrison and Manitoba water systems.

subsubtopic: MINISTERIAL DISCUSSION OF POSSIBLE PROSECUTIONS- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for unanimous consent of the House to move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity.
Considering the unusual procedure confirmed yesterday by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Lawrence) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) regarding the laying of charges under the combines act, where the Prime Minister approved a practice whereby the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs discussed the laying of charges with the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski), which was never the practice in the past, and considering that under section 15 of the combines act the director of investigation is to have complete independence, following an inquiry, to refer a case to the Attorney General for the purpose of laying charges, without any political influence or considerations, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray):
That the Prime Minister conduct an immediate investigation into this case to determine who was present at the said meeting, what was said, and whether everything was according to law and practice, and that until the Prime Minister reports to the House on this important matter, he suspend the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs from his functions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. I wish him well in his important responsibilities.
1 know that his government has made a fetish of consultation with the provinces, even in areas where the provinces have little or no jurisdiction. Certainly this is the case in the allocation of quotas between types of fishing fleets.
May I ask the minister if he would inform his colleague from New Brunswick who immediately complained that he had not been consulted. I suspect that those who were consulted and agreed were from provinces where large fleets have dominated inshore fisheries policies for years. Has the minister considered that a lot of small fishermen belonging to fragmented organizations do not sit on the Atlantic Groundfish Advisory Committee, and in fact that he as minister should make sure that their interest is served, and not only the interest of the large fleet based outside the Gulf?

I want to say to the hon. gentleman that I take second place to no one, not even the hon. member, in looking after the interests of the inshore fishermen. I say to him that consultation does not necessarily mean agreement, but there was consultation. On the basis of that consultation, we took our responsibility and made a decision.
I am sorry the hon. member does not agree with the decision taken, but it was made on the basis of updated biological data. I had no choice but to allocate those additional quotas. I was advised, after consultation with the inshore fishermen, that they could only use an additional 4,000 metric tons. After consultation with the non-Gulf fleet, they wanted the remaining 9,000 and we agreed to allocate them 6,000 metric tons because they had been fishing anyway for the same stock off Sydney Bight. That now means they will be, of course, able to fish in the Gulf in November and December at a time when there will be no inshore fishing activity in any event.

-one of a series of meetings thal take place quite frequently in regard to various prosecutions recommended by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to the Minister of Justice.

Yesterday the hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) put this question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark). The answer by the Prime Minister is alarming. The hon. member for Burnaby said to the Prime Minister:
Will the right hon. Prime Minister also confirm to the House that there will be no further such involvement, particularly by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, in discussing possible charges of price-fixing by oil companies under the Combines Investigation Act?
As we all know, there is an inquiry going on with respect to the oil companies and that is just about ready for prosecution. What did the Prime Minister answer when asked to give assurance that there will be no further discussions? He said:
Mr. Speaker, if I properly interpret the question put by the hon. member, he is asking that I guarantee that before the government takes action, ministers who might have a particular interest in an action that would be taken should not be consulted. Naturally, 1 am not going to give that kind of guarantee.
The Prime Minister is saying that he will not guarantee that these kinds of discussions will go on any further. That is a shocking thing under our tradition with respect to prosecutions as they are carried out by attorneys general of this country and carried out by the director of investigation under the Combines Act.
I should point out that the director of investigation under the Combines Act is not an ordinary civil servant. He has statutory powers under the Combines Act to act independently, without any pressures or influence or any sort of political discussion. Therefore, not only would I support the hon. member for Burnaby in his question of privilege that this be referred for full investigation to see who was there, what was said, and how many meetings there were, but I go back to the question 1 put to the Prime Minister. I believe this minister should be suspended until this whole thing is settled.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan Lawrence (Solicitor General and Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: MR. ROBINSON (BURNABY)-MINISTERIAL ANSWERS DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not know if there was going to be another ex-minister making a contribution to this debate. As I understand the situation, and

October 17, 1979
Privilege-Mr. S. Robinson
I am sorry that 1 received no official notification whatsoever that a question of privilege would arise today on this matter, there is a request that if there is a valid question of privilege that has been enunciated before you that you refer this matter to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. 1 may say to you that certainly I would have no objection for that to be done if you thought you had genuine cases of privilege before you.
Again, 1 had nothing from the Chair, the Table or the hon. member about this matter. However, as 1 understand the question of privilege that has been enunciated to you, it is a double-barrelled one. Number one, there has been some tinkering with the official journals of this House in relation to Hansard of yesterday. If that is true, that is a very serious charge to make. Certainly 1 would like to see that cleared up. Second, somehow or other in the course of the question periods of Friday, Monday, and yesterday, I intentionally misled the House. Basically I think those are the two portions of the question of privilege before you.
Let me deal with the first one first. In no manner, shape or form have I corrected Hansard at all, or attempted to correct Hansard at all in respect of anything that I said yesterday or the day before, with the possible exception of some very gross grammatical errors that I have the habit of making in this House, but certainly in respect of any question of substance referred to by the hon. member, I can indicate to you, sir, to the House, and to the member, that 1 have not changed or intended to change Hansard in any way, and in relation to the phraseology used by the member I have no knowledge whatsoever of that type of change being made.
As a matter of fact, in respect of both versions which the hon. member has just given to the House, my impression and my memory are that both of those are wrong. Not only is Hansard wrong, but also in respect of the tape which the hon. member says he heard in respect of what I said-I think that was wrong, because what I intended to say, and what I believe I did say in respect of this question, and the knowledge of my colleague in respect of this matter, was that the meeting that we held last Friday, a meeting by the way that was not even called by me, was the first opportunity that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) had of being apprised of the facts of this matter.
That meeting was not called by me. It was called by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Flynn) pursuant to his responsibilities and his duties. The ex-minister said that type of meeting had never been called before. 1 believe he is wrong. In any event, that type of meeting had been held before. As a matter of fact, in regard to possible prosecutions under the Combines Investigation Act, that type of consultation has taken place not only under this administration but under previous administrations.
In respect of the advice that was given to the Minister of Transport, which is the crucial point referred to by the member referring to alterations in Hansard, I sent a brief to the Minister of Transport which I have reason to believe he unfortunately received just as he was going to that meeting, and that meeting was the first time in an information-giving

session such as that the Minister of Transport had any opportunity to be aware of the meeting at all.
That is the type of impression I intended to leave with the House when I said what I said, and I firmly believe that is exactly what I did say. If the hon. member is now saying that I said something different from that, I am saying that the hon. member is totally wrong.
Getting back to the other question, the question of me misleading the House in respect of previous meetings, I say to the ex-minister that if he does not know that this is not a discretionary matter for the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, he should know it is not a discretionary matter.
It is not me who the director of investigations has to convince to proceed with an action in that case. It is not me who the Minister of Transport or any other operating departmental head has to convince. The question whether or not there is to be a prosecution under the Combines Investigation Act is a matter solely and exclusively within the responsibility of the Attorney General of Canada.
I believe the Minister of Justice is making a speech today, perhaps in the other place-I am not sure-clearly indicating that it is his responsibility, and to know more about the intended prosecution he wanted, of course, to consult with me; he wanted to consult with the director, he wanted to consult with the minister and, as a matter of fact, he wanted to consult with another minister, the minister whose responsibilities involve federal-provincial relations, because in regard to the western trucking situation what has to be done, because of governmental intervention into the whole question of rate setting and the whole question of route setting, has to involve some direct and open consultation with provincial ministers. To indicate that this type of consultation with this government should not be carried on by anyone, even with other governments, is a completely ridiculous notion.
I was very interested to hear three different ex-ministers say that it is not within the responsibility of the Attorney General of Canada to consult with other ministers before he starts a prosecution. That is utter nonsense. I happen to believe it is utter nonsense within the knowledge of the ex-minister who just interrupted me, not to mention two or three other ministers. I say this because I can well remember, in this very chamber, the attorney general of Canada, who at the time was a certain hon. member, Ronald Basford, indicating on March 17, 1978, that as attorney general of the day he had consulted with certain of his ministerial colleagues before instructing that charges be laid against the Toronto Sun, its editor and its publisher, under the Official Secrets Act.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. ROBINSON (BURNABY)-MINISTERIAL ANSWERS DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext:
I have no intention of prolonging this discussion. The hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) has raised by way of a question of privilege a matter which contains three points-it has been described as having two but essentially it contains three, none of which, I think, falls within the definition of privilege following the intervention by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Lawrence).
First, is the question of the possible alteration in Hansard. I have had a preliminary investigation undertaken and the line to which the hon. member for Burnaby refers may have been misread by the reporter-I am not sure-but 1 will certainly undertake to the House to investigate, as I always do, and report to the House. Any alteration in Hansard is, of course, a very serious matter. But that is a subject for me to take up, now, with the editor in the light of the minister's assertion that at no time did he effect any alteration in the record. Once the minister has not done so, if it is the editor or the reporters, that is the responsibility of the Chair, and I will investigate the matter and make a full report at the earliest opportunity.
The other two points relate to whether or not it is a proper practice for ministers to consult with one another before laying a prosecution under the Combines Investigation Act. While that is a fascinating point, it is not a procedural point. Whether or not ministers are taking a step which is not in keeping with precedent in terms of ministerial practice is a matter of some concern and interest to hon. members, I am sure, but whether they do so, or whether they propose to continue to do so, may become a matter of legality or a matter of constitutional significance, even. However, it is surely not a matter of procedural significance here in the House; it is not a question of privilege whether ministers do or do not consult before the director of prosecutions gives advice to the Attorney General of Canada on the initiation of proceedings under that particular statute. Therefore, since it is not a procedural matter, there is no point our continuing argument as to whether or not consultations of that kind can take place or have taken place in the past. It does not give rise to a question of privilege, at least not in the manner in which it has been cast today.
Finally, there is the question of whether or not the minister misled the House. He has stated he stands by what he says, that it was a correct explanation of the information he pos-
Privilege-Mr. Fox
sessed at the time. Presumably he invites hon. members to check the record to see what it says and whether it conforms to the information he now has. From the procedural point of view the significance is that the minister stands by what he said. Therefore, if any misleading took place, it was obviously misleading which was not intentional.
Members who examine the precedents will understand that if a question of privilege is to be established here the House must not only have been misled by the minister but the House must have been misled intentionally. Whether he was right or wrong, the minister says he stands by his answer. Therefore, if any misleading took place-which he denies-then obviously that misleading could not have been intentional in the circumstance. Whether this becomes a matter for debate or argument, or criticism of the quality of the answer given, or criticism of the performance of the minister, remains, again, an open question. What I have to decide is whether or not there is a procedural matter involved. The only circumstance in which it can become a procedural matter involving privilege would be if the minister deliberately misled the House and, since the minister stands by his answer, obviously he could not have deliberately misled the House if, indeed, he misled the House at all, which he denies.
For these reasons, having examined the three points which were raised, I do not think any useful purpose can be served by continuing the discussion at this time.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ENERGY REPORTED INCREASE PROPOSED IN PRICES OF OIL AND GASOLINE
MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ENERGY REPORTED INCREASE PROPOSED IN PRICES OF OIL AND GASOLINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), to move the adjournment of the House under the provisions of Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing an important and specific matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the reported proposed increase of $4

per barrel a year for oil and, more specifically, an increase of 24 cents to 30 cents a gallon in the price of gasoline now being proposed by the Government of Canada to the ten provinces, which will have a catastrophic impact on the Canadian economy resulting in massive inflation and unemployment and triggering an economic recession affecting all regions of Canada.
It is imperative that, before implementation, this House of Commons urgently and immediately discuss this alarming Government of Canada proposal.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ENERGY REPORTED INCREASE PROPOSED IN PRICES OF OIL AND GASOLINE
speechtext:
Order. I have received in proper time the notice of the hon. member of his intention to seek the invocation of Standing Order 26 in order to arrange an emergency debate on the subject he has just outlined to the House, and his presentation is in keeping with the notice which he did give me.
I do not feel that this is a proper subject for discussion at this time pursuant to Standing Order 26, for several reasons. The first is that I have some doubt as to whether it is necessary to set up an emergency debate to discuss anything during the course of the throne speech debate when any member can seek the floor and raise any subject he believes is relevant to the Speech from the Throne. 1 would not have ruled the matter aside on that point alone, because there are obvious restrictions on the ability of a group of members to address themselves to a subject in a cohesive way during the throne speech debate, but, after all, I must have regard for the fact that the hon. member and his colleagues do have an opportunity to participate in the balance of the throne speech debate and to focus on this subject if it is their desire to do so.
I have some other doubts, though, which lead me, on balance, not to grant the application. I have some concern as to whether this is on an ongoing matter rather than a matter of critical proportions. We have several problems of this sort. Members seek to utilise the provisions of Standing Order 26 on various problems in the country such as unemployment, inflation, and matters of that nature which are continuing problems but which, members allege, at a given time cross from being chronic to acute problems worthy of emergency consideration. Oil prices are a continuing matter in that category, and it would be very difficult to persuade me that continuing or chronic considerations are, or ever were, intended to be the proper subject of Standing Order 26. However, even if they were, in this particular case I have further doubts.
I am sure that even on a cursory examination of the news reports related to the subject which the hon. member has raised, price increases, as usual, would be for a future date, and in fact would not be at one time but would be phased in over a rather extended period of time. All of that obviously has to be taken into account when considering whether the House will have an opportunity to discuss these.
It remains unclear as to whether the government, in proposing the price increases, either requires or, even if it does not require, intends to seek the approval of Parliament. That remains uncertain for me now, and in any case in the final analysis it has been said, and was repeated again today by the
October 17, 1979

Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie), that the price increase for crude oil itself does not require parliamentary approval.
The hon. member has included in his motion, and I quote more specifically "an increase of 24 cents to 30 cents a gallon". That, I understand on the basis of the replies of the Minister of Finance here in the House, relates to a suggested increase in the federal tax which would, 1 gather, be coupled with any such increase about which the hon. member is concerned. If that is so, that would clearly be a budgetary measure and would be debated in full during the course of a budget presentation. Therefore, 1 have to conclude that the House would not, on the information 1 have now, be deprived in any way of ample opportunity to debate the matters raised in this application, if in fact they do come about, which was left in some uncertainty today.
Therefore, until some of these matters are clarified more completely, I would not be disposed to think the House should consider this matter as an emergency pursuant to my understanding of Standing Order 26.
The House resumed, from Tuesday, October 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fretz for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I take this opportunity, which is my first to rise to speak in this Thirty-first Parliament, to congratulate you on your re-election as Speaker. I had the opportunity in my first session of Parliament to have you as a neighbour, a row ahead of me, and I remember those days very well. Your wit and your wisdom have only increased since that time, and they were at a very high standard then.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I would also like, in the spirit of this House in its better moments-and we will start off with the better moments and see how it goes through my speech-to offer my congratulations to the new Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) and hon. members opposite on the mandate given them in the election. I want to talk about the degree of that mandate as I make my comments today, but as best I can I sincerely wish them well in the interest of Canada.
I want to congratulate both the mover, the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz), and the seconder of the address in reply, the
The Address-Mr. Fleming
hon. member for Cardigan (Mr. MacDonald). Their thoughtful comments about their constituencies, their firmness of mind and freshness bode well for their contributions to this Parliament in the months ahead.
I plan to deal with two areas. First, as a member of the opposition and a member of Parliament since 1972, 1 would like to deal with the commitments made by the new government during the course of the last election campaign and what we now have instead. As well, 1 want to deal with the cultural field, in which I was given some opportunity by my leader to concentrate in an area which I believe is absolutely fundamental and critical to the survival of this nation.
I should like to speak on the issue of the new government, about what they promised and what we have. May I review, if I can, some of their economic proposals. They said that the last government, the government of which I was a supporter, had created terrible deficits, that indeed the spending of the Government of Canada was sending Canada down the road to hell. And so, in the course of the last campaign they concocted as an answer something called the stimulative deficit. That was created by that great democrat, Senator de Cotret. The senator proposed that, and that is what we heard in the campaign. Upon their election and in a minority situation, they abandoned that as impossible because they said matters were even worse than they thought they were so far as deficits were concerned. That is a possible position to take, except that that particular declaration, while abandoning a major plan that offered the return of money to many Canadians who felt the tax burden was becoming unduly large, that rationalization, came the same week that another senior minister of the new government announced that the deficit for the current fiscal year would be less than that forecast by the previous government.
In turn, the previous government was accused of being gutless and unimaginative on several very basic economic principles followed by that previous government. We were attacked for persistently claiming to float the dollar and, in fact, not floating it. I can remember when, day after day, the then member for Don Valley, now the principal economic adviser to the new Prime Minister, would rise in the House and attack the minister of finance of the last government, saying, "You are not floating the dollar at all; you are interfering with hundreds of millions of dollars; you are meddling with it. Fix it or float it. 1 would like to have it fixed." 1 believe that is what he said. He said, "1 would like to have it fixed, but make up your mind." Upon forming the government in the six months that followed, they followed precisely the same policy they had constantly attacked when they were in opposition.
When it comes to the traditional policy of recent Canadian governments to increase our interest rate in line with increases in the American interest rate in order to attract capital and to grow as a country, we were constantly attacked for following the Americans, for not having some independence of mind, and for not finding an alternate course. Of course what we have seen happen since the election is again the policy they attacked

October 17, 1979
The Address-Mr. Fleming
as a fundamental mistake on our side which they have now decided to follow. They followed it religiously, even though there are many of us on this side who believe the time has come now to investigate at least, to see if it is wise, simply without questioning, to follow the increases in the American rate, especially when our own inflation rate is considerably lower than that of the Americans and we may indeed have a possible alternative policy that could work for Canada.
At any rate, on all these fronts, on the promised spending and give-out to the taxpayers, on the issue of the floating or non-floating dollar, on the issue of our inflation rates, they promised the opposite of what we were doing, but all they have done since they have formed the government is exactly what we did. I suggest that placed in the minds of the Canadian public, now that Parliament has finally met, some real concern about credibility and some real doubts that there would be some changes. Obviously the outcome of the election showed that some change was desired. That is what they said they would give, but apparently in those fundamental areas they will not give it at all.
They also accused us of being insensitive-and this was through the other side of the mouth-when we proposed the tightening up of the unemployment insurance regulations, because there was a broad feeling in the land, and a feeling in this House among members of most of the parties at least, that systems which were well intended were not working well. So, 1 must say that after considerable debate in my own caucus in the last Parliament, some changes were put forward, and those changes, finally after lengthy debate, were adopted, but with the then official opposition opposing us on that issue. What is the first thing they did upon becoming government? They gave final approval to putting those changes into effect!
I am talking about credibility and the very difficult position of the Canadian public as we try to make this Parliament work. During the campaign 1 heard a great deal about wage and price controls, about the last campaign five years earlier, the 1974 campaign. I heard about how we promised something and did a complete reversal. Well, at least it took us 18 months and very changed economic circumstances to do a reversal. They, in three or four months, reversed on almost every major economic plank they had, and the ones where they have not, 1 find most incredible as an offering to this Parliament for Canada's future.
I should like to mention one or two economic issues such as the issue of cuts to the civil service, the so called privatization. As 1 recall, that began by the Progressive Conservative Party saying. "You have too much government. We are going to cut it down. It is too much of a burden. The people are paying too much in taxes and the deficits are too great." They said, "Our answer will be a cut of 60,000." That is a nice figure; it has lots of zeros in it, but how they came up with the six in front I do not know. They got rid of Bryce Mackasey and that leaves them with 59,999. However, they say they have a plan.
That mastermind-I know he does not like to hear it said- the mastermind of the bank of western Canada, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens), continues to demon-

strate his ability as one of Canada's leading economic acrobats. In the minds of the Canadian public these cuts are going to mean less of a burden on the taxpayer, and yet he is suggesting that one of the major Crown corporations the government should get rid of is a company like de Havilland with several thousand workers from my own constituency, a Crown corporation that a Liberal federal government took over in order to build it, to concentrate on technology which could be a world competitor and to make it strong. That is happening; it has just begun to show a reasonable profit. But what do they do? They say they will get rid of it. Well, there are two problems with that. First, that will not help the pocketbook of the Canadian taxpayer because the company is making profit and it is in the interests of the Canadian public to retain that company, at least until it reaches the point of considerably greater health. Right now it is at the turning point of real expansion and real success, and we will have to watch very closely as the new government moves toward privatization of de Havilland, to be sure that indeed the long-term interest of that technology and the interests of those workers are kept in mind.
Much the same can be said of Canadair. Here is a company we picked up as the federal Liberal government. We said it needs help, it needs some direction and money for support. We gave it support and now it is highly successful, but they say, with some kind of crazy economics, "Now that it is successful, we will give it back to the private sector and let someone else profit rather than the taxpayers of Canada."
One other economic issue of some importance to me, coming as I do from metropolitan Toronto, is the so-called mortgage interest tax deduction program. That program has now been switched to a mortgage interest tax credit. In my view, that is a positive step. Their original plan would have meant that the richer you are, if you hold a mortgage the more you will get. Now it means you will all get the same amount. I must admit that must come as some disappointment to some of the folks who voted Conservative and, after adding and subtracting, figured they would get as much as $4,000 or $5,000. Now the maximum they will get is $1,500 after the program is phased in.
Of much more concern to me, however, are those people who rent, the old and middle-aged people who worked hard to pay off their mortgages. Of much more concern to me in my constituency are the many thousands of Canadians who have built their homes here, particularly when I think of the Italian Canadian community and others who, very quickly, believing it was fundamental to their family life to have their home paid for, paid off their mortgages in less than ten years, pooling their resources, working hard, scrubbing floors, putting up brick walls, helping to build our cities. They will get nothing out of this program, and yet it is the major offering to the Canadian public, so far as getting any money back is concerned. Where will all that money come from to pay back the terrible deficits which this government says we have created?
October 17, 1979

Perhaps I have said enough about economics, unless one considers the Jerusalem embassy issue an economic one. 1 do not know how, at least in part, it can be considered anything else. Surely the kindest thing which can be said about that whole terrible mess and all its consequences is that it was an ill thought out decision of no real aid to Israel. Perhaps in the long term it would be against the interests of Israel. Certainly it has caused us great trouble in the Arab world. How many millions or billions have we lost? When they talked about the policy of moving the embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem, I heard nothing about the much touted promise of the previous Conservative opposition that when taking government they would bring down a tough Arab boycott bill, that they would really do something. I wonder if anyone else has heard anything about that.
The government I supported put forward a bill which the Jewish community that supports Israel directly, and generally the Canadian community, found to be a reasonable approach. It was a guarantee that certainly we were not going to allow any discrimination against people because of their faith or interest in Israel. Certainly if that happened, it would be public and it would be castigated. There would be pressure against the people who might do that. All of a sudden with respect to something about which there was not enough before, we have heard nothing since.
We had the promise of an open government. Certainly for five months there was no Parliament. Now we have a Parliament, and when we finally get to Parliament what has the spokesman for open government and his supporters done? I gather they talked it over. 1 hope they talked it over before the Prime Minister said to Newfoundland that, even though the federal government and that province argued before, even though there was an agreement with the maritime provinces, and even though there was a test case regarding the west coast in the supreme court, the resources were theirs-"Newfoundland, here you go". After having said to the west coast, "Although we have some problems, British Columbia, here you go", he thought he might as well say it to the maritimes as well.
So there is the open government; there is the better use of Parliament. There was no reference to Parliament, no constitutional meeting. If it was open, at least we would know if they talked it over with Bill Davis. Did they talk it over with Hatfield? Did they talk it over with the Manitoba government? They are all good Conservative regimes. From what I know, no. That is our new open government. What about basic constitutional reform? I do not think anyone in the House would deny the people of Newfoundland maximizing what is justly theirs under the constitution. But the fiscal powers, and some basic interest to make sure that the fundamentals of one nation and the equality of all people in that nation are maintained, must be retained for the central government, the government of all Canadians.
When we talk about open government we should remember that two-thirds of the cabinet are locked out of the inner
The Address-Mr. Fleming
cabinet. That is not a very open government. Coming from Toronto I should like to ask where is Toronto in this inner cabinet? Where is Manitoba? My leader pointed that out very well. Where is New Brunswick in that inner group? We have had a tough season in Toronto, aside from my party having lost some seats, which is perhaps a non-objective comment. But the Argos have not been doing very well, the Argos wearing their blue. The Blue Jays wearing their blue have not done very well, and now we have the blue Tory ministers, all of them second string. Poor Toronto is not doing very well, although I have some hope for the Argos. Hope springs eternal, and I have some long range hope for the Blue Jays.

speechtext: What about the blue maple leaf?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I do not know about those three fellows from Toronto sitting on the outside. 1 do not know if they have a hope at all of getting into first place.
Then there is Petro-Canada. I see we have brought hon. members opposite to life a little. That always encourages me. They will not disband Petro-Canada; they will simply cut off its arms and legs. Well, they will keep the high risk part in order to go out and spend money that others will not spend in frontier areas and to develop the tar sands and to find the technology to give us a real assurance of energy supply for the future. They will keep that part and sell off the profitable part. Meanwhile they con the public by giving them free shares. It looks like that will happen. After that the little guy will have a few shares. He can watch them go up as his taxes and energy costs go up. Then the big guy will buy shares. He will buy shares and make profits, and we will have a great Canadian company! Is that not wonderful? It is, but what about energy prices for average Canadians? What about pensioners trying to heat their homes? What about poor people? Where is our expertise, which we cannot just have in the high risk portion, to know the entire market place, to know whether we are being conned by some of those multinationals? It is gone.
I guess we have heard a great deal about Petro-Canada. Perhaps members on both sides are becoming tired of hearing the word. I do not believe anyone can say that the retention of Pacific Pete, the Atlantic Richfield portion, the profitable part, will harm the Canadian public. After messing up Jerusalem, after changing all their financial proposals, after keeping Liberal policies which they frowned on for months and years, how can they say finally that they will show guts by taking up that policy on a fundamental issue of interest to all Canadians, which I am sure no one can deny? It is madness. If it is madness today, then it will be a lot more madness a year or two down the road when this Parliament finds itself back in an election. Woe is the day as that story unravels for that party and that government. As that tragedy unravels, woe is the day for the Canadian public.
Even Bill Davis is shaking in his boots today. A couple of months ago Mr. Davis went out with his animated face and charged around the province of Ontario supporting the new Prime Minister. We know that he must be sitting quietly at home now, perhaps with a glass of brandy in one hand,

October 17, 1979
The Address-Mr. Fleming
wondering if everything in his past has been all that correct and wise.
I have said enough about Petro-Canada, but before I pass on to another topic I should like to make reference to Foothills. It was to provide $1.5 billion to $2 billion and tens of thousands of jobs for Canada. Apparently over the period of three months no minister, no prime minister, or no senior official had a meeting with Foothills. During the months of June, July and August there were no meetings in the new government over a major Canadian economic need. It was a matter that was by no means assured. Everyone watching the United States knew the confrontation between the executive and the legislative branch and did not think for a moment that it should not be watched. They knew there was public relations and leaning and pushing to do. The Conservative government, the experts on business, the ones who want privatization, did nothing over three months. Zip, it went out the window, and, "gosh, oh golly, shucks," another one is gone. If one looks at Japan, apparently Japan is out the window.
We have read about Argentina in the last few weeks. We have read about the Middle East and the Mexican deal. There was to be a meeting in September, and the Prime Minister made a joke. Somebody said, "Postponed or cancelled?" The Prime Minister said, "No, just postponed until next year". I do not know if we will be on our feet economically next year if this kind of record continues.
1 have finished my comments about the government generally, but I should like to move to a more positive and hopeful tone, the field of culture. I mean that sincerely. 1 want to congratulate the Secretary of State and Minister of Communications (Mr. MacDonald). He is not here today, he is away at a conference with his provincial counterparts who have responsibilities for communications. I want to pay my respects. In the cultural community he is considered progressive. Last November 1 believe he indicated in the budget speech five or six budgetary proposals which he said were commitments of his party to assist the Canadian cultural community if they got into office. He and his committee on culture moved across the country last year. I believe it showed a real desire to make some progress. In that speech the then hon. member for Egmont said the following:
Our institutions of culture are starved for funding ... such neglect of our culture ... can only seriously jeopardize the well-being of this nation. We must bring a new vigour to federal responsibility.
If one honestly cared about one's country and is a critic in that area, then one would look forward to new vigour. I know of the minister's sincerity. I would call him a progressive more than a conservative in his interests in the field of culture, but he is not a superman. He is not faster than a speeding bullet. He cannot leap tall buildings in one bound. Also, he is the inner cabinet minister for social policy. What is that? Is it medicare? Do we have problems with medicare? Is there slippage? Will it not be universal any more? He is responsible for that in the inner cabinet. Also native interests are major responsibilities. There are big problems to be solved fairly. Also I gather that pensions will come under his inner cabinet

responsibilities. What about indexing? Are we not to have indexing? Will we fight to keep indexing so that old people will not have less and less each year? What about social assistance? He has all of that to handle, as well as communications. There are staggering challenges over satellites, cable television, Pay TV, interconnections, super stations, and the future of the CRTC and its ability to cope. He is faced with all of those challenges. Then we come to the field of culture where he says we need new vigour.
Then we have the CBC. Do we have problems with the CBC? Do we have problems with the CBC! Then we have the National Film Board, the Canadian Film Development Corporation, the National Arts Centre, the Canada Council, with all its implications, the National Museums, the National Gallery, which is very important, the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council, the National Library, as well as publishing policy and recording policy. On and on the list goes, with one human being to deal with them all. No matter how progressive or how capable, how can he do it? Why when they have 137 members, and 1 mean this genuinely, with some very competent people in the back benches, is it necessary? Is he the only progressive man, in the Prime Minister's mind? Is this one of the few red Tories holding on? I hope that is not the case. I want good things in the cultural area, but why is one minister trying to cope with so much? He is a man who does care and understand.

speechtext: He is so good.

speechtext: Well, we will find out in time. I think that is arrogance on the part of this inner cabinet minister who suggests he is so good, and he is so good. He is so good there is no room for the others I think are very good and should be there.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No, my colleague.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I quite understood the "so good" minister.
Let me take a moment now to deal with the parliamentary enquiry that was very vaguely referred to in the throne speech. We do not know if it will be a joint parliamentary enquiry of the Senate and the Commons, though I have heard it will be that, I believe in a speech by the new Secretary of State and Minister of Communications. The idea of putting all the cultural fields together, reviewing things and straightening it all out, is something that everyone who is involved in the area has been calling for now for a year or two. I know the previous secretary of state made several major efforts at putting them together. I have real concern in a minority Parliament whether this can be competently and thoughtfully done when we are faced with the workload and the challenges we have here.
Of equal concern is the fear that while the Secretary of State and Minister of Communications may feel that is a productive route, and that demonstrates democratization and the open government concept they want to prove, it may be very dangerous, indeed, when the minister who just interjected
October 17, 1979

a moment ago can go in and argue as President of the Treasury Board that it is under study and they do not need any more money. Remember, it was the Secretary of State who said a year ago that they were starving. Let us not continue that starvation. We take him at his word, but is that not a good excuse? That is what I am afraid of, that he will say they are having a study and that they should not be given any money until that study is completed. How long will that study take, and how much more critical will the situation become? The Secretary of State has said the situation is critical.
Let me take a moment to talk about this suggestion about starvation for funding. 1 asked my first question of the Secretary of State and Minister of Communications last week and he very proudly, when I questioned the heavy burden he had, responded that he had found $2 million more for the Canada Council. That was not responding to the question. 1 am very pleased about the $2 million, as I know it is a breath of air for them, but it is still $6 million to $7 million less than they would have had without restraint. It was the previous government that I supported that brought in restraint. While 1 was in support of that government, I also criticized it in committee for the extent of the restraint. I support the new minister in giving them more assistance.
If that is $2 million more, whatever happened to that $24 million the previous secretary of state, Mr. Roberts, promised from Loto Canada funds? We now hear that the total deal back is $24 million, and that is for sports and culture. If we have half of that, that is $12 million, and $12 million and $2 million is $14 million, we end up with a net loss of $10 million, and that is for the cultural community. But I will bet anything 1 can bet that it is not going to be $12 million. My hint for that was in a letter I received in response to a letter I sent to the Secretary of State. In that letter of September 19 he said:
The net result will be increased revenues available from Canadian lotteries for the support of sports and cultural activity. That these new funds will be realized primarily at the provincial level is in my opinion a most positive development toward encouraging more active provincial participation in cultural support.
I agree, the provinces have to do more. Of course they do. He seems to be saying there will be more money, but not here. He seems to be suggesting it is for the provinces. More money for the provinces is good, but he says we are starving here, suggesting that the Canada Council and all those other agencies are starving. This letter seems to suggest less money, not more money, and I think the cultural community, which has some faith in this new minister, deserves an answer. Is the amount to be $10 million less, $12 million less or $14 million less? If it is $10 million more I will be very happy and the first to congratulate the new minister. However, I have my fears about that.
The proposals of November, 1978, put forward by the new Secretary of State, included expanding the 100 per cent capital cost allowance for publishing and recording. I argued, as I did under a motion pursuant to Standing Order 43 last week, that he said last November these firmly would be budgetary proposals if they formed the government. They formed the government early last May, or early last June, and they have had
The Address-Mr. Fleming
five months to introduce them. We still do not know the budget date, but there is no secret about these things. That party promised them. We have a starved cultural community. Why not bring them in or bring them forward for discussion in committee so we can find out if they will work? They may not work, but I would like to find out about them. I want to be positive, but why put them off and then say they are starving?
I do not think that is fair to a community that holds hope in this minister. I do not think this was rhetoric in opposition. Perhaps the problem is that he cannot get his colleagues to move. If he cannot, 1 want to point out that there is a problem.
I want to talk for a moment, if I may, about the suggestions contained in the minister's speeches when he was a member of the opposition and the critic of the then secretary of state. He seemed to suggest that he would regionalize the National Film Board and the Canada Council. I have heard around and about, in talking to people and in interviewing them, in an attempt to pick up the best knowledge I can about this area in addition to what I have learned over the years as a member of Parliament, that he has abandoned that. I hope he has, because strong regions do not have to mean a weakening of the middle, and if they do mean a weakening of the middle I think that is catastrophic. I hope that is not the direction he is going.
There are some specific areas in respect of which I want to put some questions on the record. Let me refer to the area of copyright. My colleague, the hon. member for Argenteuil (Mr. Gourd) very forcefully made the point during the throne speech debate yesterday that for 50 years, and to the discredit of the previous government as well, no changes have been made in the Copyright Act. He referred to all the disadvantages it creates for our authors when we are trying to spur our Canadian authors and to build Canadian talent. Some real efforts were made by the last secretary of state. I know a lot was happening in his office to press the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, where the responsibility lies, for some action in this regard. I simply want to say that while our committee has not formally reached an agreement on that policy, and this involves simply a matter of finding the time in the first few weeks, I agree entirely with my colleague, and I hope we will move in that direction. I hope we can pressure the government into moving in that direction.
Again a major area of criticism by the new Secretary of State was in respect of copyright and the lack of action. He has been the Secretary of State for almost six months. In looking at 80 new bills on the order paper, some of them not so new, 1 see nothing about copyright.
Let me refer to voluntary action, an area of concern and the responsibility of the Secretary of State. We read in the papers that Ken Dryden has left the nets to do a little protective work. Perhaps I should be more positive. He has left to do some investigative work in the voluntary action area. He is going to head up a task force on voluntary action. When we call the department we are told they know nothing about it. There are no terms of reference, and they have not seen Mr. Dryden.
There was a task force on voluntary action several years ago. I simply want to encourage the Secretary of State, with

October 17, 1979
The Address-Mr. R. Richardson
the support of his government, to move quickly on this. I have some agreement with members opposite that good work can be done in the voluntary sector, and it is time we found out about these concerns. It is time we found out specifically whether lotteries, for instance, have distorted the ability of the voluntary sector.
1 asked questions on that of the last government. I have written to the new Secretary of State, and I am very pleased that he has replied saying he shares these concerns and will be pleased to explore this issue more fully. He is going to take it up with his cabinet colleagues. He has asked for my suggestions, and I have suggested he certainly should look into the social impact of lotteries.
Finally, in conclusion, I simply want to say culture is not an airy-fairy issue; it is the reality of Canada. Of course the regions have to maximize and reflect the reality to themselves, but we are more than regions and we are more than a community of communities. We are a nation, and each part of Canada helps to make up the greatness of the total, but each part must better learn of, understand, and appreciate the other parts. It is the sharing of the richness of diversity that leads to national maturity. It is the assurance of the opportunity for excellence to develop anywhere that guarantees artistic and cultural opportunity everywhere.

speechtext: Hear, hear!
