speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first most sincerely congratulate you on the unanimous selection of yourself for a difficult but most important post. I can think of no better person for this most respected position during what I am certain all hon. members will work for and pray will be a Parliament of Reconciliation." I pledge to you my co-operation in this essential task.
Next, I extend the traditional and very sincere congratulations to the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz) and the hon. member for Cardigan (Mr. MacDonald) who moved and seconded the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne.
I should also like to refer to my predecessor, the member for the riding of Greenwood, Mr. Andrew Brewin, and pay a tribute to him. Mr. Brewin is a very fine gentleman, a respected parliamentarian who represented my district for 17 years and, in my opinion, he is a compassionate man and a great Canadian.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I hope to hold a reception for him later this year here on the Parliament Hill he loved so well, to which all of his many friends will be invited. I should like this House to know that Andrew Brewin is held in high regard and affection by many who, like myself, do not happen to share his political views.
I should also like to express my personal tribute to the memory of the Right Hon. John George Diefenbaker who was well known to the Richardson family. As some hon. members

would know, my uncle, Burt Richardson, was Mr. Diefenbak-er's chief of staff for several years in the early 1960's. Mr. Diefenbaker was a man of great moral integrity and personal courage-a man of strong Christian conviction-and my only regret is that I did not have the privilege to sit in this House with him as a member of this Thirty-first Parliament.
My sadness at the passing of Mr. Diefenbaker is only the human feeling of realizing a great man and former prime minister of the Canada we love is no longer with us. It is more than overcome by the knowledge that the present Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) and leader of this Progressive Conservative government is equally a man of great moral integrity and personal courage, who is willing and able to take the tough actions necessary to ensure a safe, prosperous and united Canada for all Canadians in the days, months and years ahead.
I propose in this speech, Mr. Speaker, to deal with the prospects for Canadian peace and prosperity raised in the Speech from the Throne and, in particular, to challenge all hon. members to work together to help restore morality and a sense of true values to public affairs. After all, Mr. Speaker, Parliament is the central forum of our country. It should set the tone of public life since its decisions are felt by every Canadian. Our greatest challenge, individually and collectively as members of Parliament, is to help rebuild public respect and confidence in government.
First, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few general remarks. At a moment like this when I am giving my first speech in this historic Parliament, I naturally think of the people in my own constituency. I think of the people of Beaches, as I am sure other hon. members think of their constituents, as the salt of the earth, and I hope I can justify the confidence they have placed in me as their federal representative.
I think particularly, Mr. Speaker, of the many people I met during the past two years of campaigning as I called from house to house, who have experienced and are experiencing the devastating effects of prolonged inflation. I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, about the retired people trying to live on limited pensions, the working men and women whose life savings arc being destroyed, the homemakers who face soaring food prices, the homeowners, merchants and other small business entrepreneurs who are being devastated by high interest rates, and the young people who are facing very uncertain job prospects.
I think also, Mr. Speaker, of the many people I met who are fed up with politics and government. I am sure other hon. members experienced the same thing. They are the people who are dismayed by corruption and scandal in high places; sick of being bought off with their own money; distressed and discouraged at red tape and remoteness of government, and downright angry about the taxes which now account at all levels of government for almost 50 per cent of all the earned income in Canada. Fifty per cent, Mr. Speaker! God only asks for 10 per cent; Caesar and his legions are not so easily satisfied.

Who can deny, Mr. Speaker, that these are darkening days? The smaller this world grows, the more it seems to fly apart. There are wars and rumours of war; hot wars, cold wars, bush wars, and economic wars. There is famine and hunger, disease and suffering, strife and turmoil. There is financial uncertainty bordering on chaos that could serve as the prelude to an awful worldwide depression with its untold misery. The threat of nuclear holocaust is constantly with us. It would seem, Mr. Speaker, that "the distress of nations" is upon us.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that primarily inflation is a moral and political problem. Have we in this House the imagination to see that it is a threat to the political, social, and moral character of our society? Do we not see that the confiscation of capital, income and savings that results from inflation provided some politicians and bureaucrats with the excuse to trespass into many areas of our lives, and curtail freedoms? Have we not perhaps now come to the point in our history where, in a very real sense, "democracy in deficit" is descriptive of both our economic plight and possibly of our political future, unless we are willing to act with courage and conviction to resolve our problems?
Mr. Speaker, I am proud to be a member of this Thirty-first Parliament and, in particular, of this new Progressive Conservative government that is facing up to these very real challenges. I trust that we all in this House perceive the need to work together, regardless of political party affiliation, to support the initiatives set out in the Speech from the Throne. We must work together, regardless of party affiliation, on the foreign policy review, on the basic reform of Parliament, and on ways to balance the budget. We must address the crucial moral issues at the heart of the human dilemma today-social justice at home and abroad, the right to life, the problem of inflation. We must come to grips with what we are all about as individuals and as a nation.
Our failure in the past as a society, and our failure specifically here in Parliament, has been to articulate our national goals and preserve our individual values in attaining them. It is this failure, Mr. Speaker, that has led to the broad sense of disillusionment amongst the Canadian people today.
1 represent many Canadian people who wish to be governed by a righteous and God-fearing Parliament. As many hon. members may be aware, Christians all over Canada have been praying for each one of you personally in the hope that men and women of God would be making the laws of the land. Mr. Speaker, I believe we have a yardstick by which to measure our effectiveness. That measuring device is God's Word. We must search for a biblical basis for civil government.
As a professional economist and businessman 1 have said much, and 1 will say more at a later time, about the primary cause of our inflation, which is government itself. But, Mr. Speaker, as a Christian and as a concerned Canadian, I am convinced that not all of Canada's problems are economic. Many are moral and spiritual. Indeed, both the human spirit and the national soul may perhaps be more in need of repair than the federal budget.
The Address-Mr. R. Richardson
I believe the bible to be true, Mr. Speaker, when it states in second Chronicles 7:14 God's promise as follows:
If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from Heaven, and will forgive their sins and will heal their lands.
What more do we need to encourage us, to motivate us, than to become active working together in the healing of our land? Mr. Speaker, I may sound like a voice crying in the wilderness, but I know for a fact that this Thirty-first Parliament has many others of like faith.
I am excited, Mr. Speaker, by much of what I have seen since the May 22 election, and I am very optimistic about our country's future because of the leadership I know will be given by hon. members in this "Parliament of Reconciliation." Our individual and national response to the desperate plight of the Vietnamese boat people, and the support received from hon. members on both sides of the House, is a very encouraging sign of what can be achieved by this Parliament as a positive witness to our fellow Canadians and to the world. Canadians have had enough of meanness and pettiness. What they want from us, Mr. Speaker, is leadership, and the true essence of leadership is service to others.
It is a fact that Canada, more than any other nation in the world, is blessed with abundant resources, good, hard working, and law abiding people, and a huge potential. As the Prime Minister has so properly said, "It is a time to build". I believe that in our Prime Minister we have an enlightened leader who has the courage of his convictions to uphold an unpopular stance in the name of the future good. He has given a positive indication in his response to the debate on the Speech from the Throne that we are and will continue to move firmly to correct those things which have been holding us back individually and collectively from meeting our God-given potential in this country. Although he would perhaps not use the same words as I, the Prime Minister has challenged us all, whether we be members of Parliament or individual Canadian citizens, to participate in this building of Canada with energy and skill; to stand fast in our faith; to fight the good fight; to be consistent in our good works, with love and understanding-"like the yeast that leavens the loaf and raises the level of all it touches".
"Do unto others as you would have them do unto you". Mr. Speaker, what a tremendous transformation would occur if the golden rule were applied to politics and government. Can you imagine the change that would be wrought? No more political campaigns based on "victory at any price by any means"; no more dog-eat-dog tactics; no more under-the-table deals; no more false witness; no more ego trips for self-centred purposes. Where there is animosity, there would be love; where there is greed, there would be generosity and compassion. Patience would take the place of anger, and service would rise above self.
Mr. Speaker, I respectfully recommend to this House that one small thing we might do to signal a new direction to the people of Canada would be to allow the general public to enter this chamber while we are conducting daily prayers. It would

October 17, 1979
The Address-Mr. Malepart
certainly do no harm, and might even prove inspirational to some Canadians to see their members of Parliament humbling themselves before God on a daily basis, asking Him for His divine guidance.
Especially in these times, Mr. Speaker, when Canada stands at the political, economic, and spiritual crossroads, the challenges facing this Parliament are very important and can be exciting and rewarding too, not in the monetary or status-seeking way, but in the knowledge that we in this House of Commons are doing our part to build Canada so that some day it might truly be said of this land that "... His dominion shall be from sea even to sea ..."
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, the challenge set out by our Fathers of Confederation was to build a nation in keeping with basic Christian principles. What began with them as a step of faith more than a century ago has proven to be a continuing test of faith ever since. I submit, Mr. Speaker, it is both a challenge and a sacred obligation for the hon. members of this House to work together in the healing of our land at this time of unparalleled opportunity.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words will be to congratulate you on your re-election as Speaker of the House and to congratulate all hon. members on their election to the House. I also want to thank all the voters in the riding of Sainte-Marie who put their confidence in me. What confidence! All other candidates lost their deposit!
Mr. Speaker, having read the Speech from the Throne, 1 have to admit that I found it very deceiving. I expected that this Progressive Conservative government, after spending 16 years in opposition claiming that it had the solutions to all our problems, would present after five months in office something other than words and pious wishes. I admit that I am deeply worried about the two million senior citizens who built this country, about the 700,000 unemployed and those who will join their ranks, and about the seven million Canadians whose income is below $10,000 because the government offers them little if anything at all.
The formation of the inner cabinet was one of the first moves made by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Clark). This category of Canadians about whom I am worried and who represent a high percentage of the population of Canada gets no consideration from this goverment. Indeed, the Prime Minister did not consider it appropriate to include in the inner cabinet the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Crombie), the Minister of Labour (Mr. Alexander), and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Atkey). Those three ministers should represent and defend the interests of the groups of Canadians they serve. It would be essential that those same ministers be present at the meetings where the main decisions are taken. I do not know why the Prime

Minister did that, whether it is because those three ministers are not competent enough or because he is simply not interested in those groups of citizens.
Mr. Speaker, 1 am convinced that if those ministers had indeed taken part in the meetings of the inner cabinet and spoken for the interests of citizens that their departments serve, the Prime Minister would certainly not contemplate increasing so quickly the price of oil. I may indicate that the first victims of that increase will be the lower income group and not the industry that can pass on this hike to those same people. Moreover, those ministers would certainly not have let the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) cut 60,000 jobs in the public service thereby increasing the number of unemployed. I would like to know on which studies the government based itself to reduce the number of civil servants by
60,000.	Can the President of the Treasury Board tell or assure the House that services offered to the public will not suffer from these cutbacks? How are we to know that there are not only 10,000 public servants too many? I trust that the decision to cut 60,000 public service jobs was not taken the day the Prime Minister decided to move the Canadian embassy to Jerusalem, because that was not his best day.
As stated in the throne speech, the government hopes to solve unemployment and create jobs by relying on the private sector. It should know that the private sector has long since had the opportunity to create jobs aided by government grants, with the result that there are now 700,000 unemployed. We have a lot to look forward to! 1 believe the government is wrong in relying only on multinationals and small and medium business, because we all know that their prime motive is profit and not job creation. One has only to consider the action taken by such companies as ITT, Cadbury, Sun Life and many others which could not care less about the workers. Often, Mr. Speaker, when governments give grants to corporations in order for them to modernize their equipment, there does not result in any new jobs. I will give you as an example a bakery with equipment producing 100 loaves of bread a minute; after receiving a grant from the federal government, they bought new equipment capable of producing 400 loaves a minute. The result is that you have only one operator instead of four, and three unemployed.
Furthermore, the Minister of Employment and Immigration decided to cut the Canada Works programs. That is unfortunate because it was one of the rare programs where the government put faith in the ordinary citizen. I hope that decision will be reviewed because in addition to creating jobs that program provided services meeting the needs of the people, particularly senior citizens. The government should also review the policy to help businesses so it will really help create employment.
Mr. Speaker, I want also draw the attention of this House to the tax credits for home owners announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie). That is an unfair decision because
October 17, 1979

there is nothing for tenants. Instead, the Government of Canada in co-operation with the provinces should have examined the possibility of establishing an over-all housing policy to help middle income workers to own a home and low income people to have decent housing through a tenant subsidy.
If you look at Statistics Canada figures for 1976, you will see that there are in Canada four million home owners versus two million tenants. If you look at the provincial breakdown there are 1,676,000 owners and 958,000 tenants in Ontario versus 953,000 owners and 940,000 tenants in Quebec. Mr. Speaker, after reading those figures, you see the government's mortgage tax credit policy is unfair to Quebec where the rate of ownership is low. Furthermore, it is also unfair to senior citizens because most of them who own a house paid off their mortgages long ago. Indeed, in an article in the newspaper La Presse of Wednesday, October 3, one can read, and I quote:
The Canadian Council on Social Development feels the interest and property tax credit program announced by the Clark government will have a very detrimental impact if it is not further improved to include low income Canadians.
In a press conference yesterday in Ottawa, Director General Pierre Bourdon urged the government to amend its program to correct its three great weaknesses which he identified as follows:
-	no advantage for tenants, who account for 37 per cent of the population;
-	a maximum tax credit of $260 after four years for families at the bottom of the income scale ($10,000 to $15,000), compared with $900 for those with an income of $30,000;
-nothing except the maximum property tax credit of $250 for owners of older houses and for rural families with large properties and low incomes.
It would have been desirable, Mr. Speaker, so as to enable middle-income Canadians to purchase a home, for the government to amend the policy of the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation which guarantees loans only for the purchase of single-family dwellings and duplexes. I refer, for instance, to the city of Montreal where the majority of houses have three floors and three or four units. If the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation could authorize guaranteed loans for these properties, we could increase the number of homeowners in Montreal, where there are now only 353,000 homeowners compared with 571,000 tenants.
As evidence of the importance of the loans guaranteed by the CMHC, if a middle-income citizen wants to buy a property evaluated at $50,000, he can obtain a 90 per cent loan guaranteed by the CMHC, which represents a mortgage of $45,000 and which means that he need only make a deposit of $5,000. However, if the loan is not guaranteed by the CMHC, he can only obtain 75 per cent ot the value ot the property, or $37,500, and must make a deposit of $12,500, which means a difference in capital of $7,500.
I also take the liberty to say to the Minister of Finance that he did not have a very good argument when he answered a reporter who told him that his policy offered nothing to tenants. He made the following answer and I quote the newspaper Le Devoir of Tuesday September 18:
The Address-Mr. Malepart
Furthermore, the Minister of Finance gives nothing to the 4.5 million tenant families because "nothing was promised to them", he said.
We cannot say it is a very brilliant answer.
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne refers to the creation of a social development ministry that will ensure better co-ordination of programs and spending in that sector. As I see it described in the Speech from the Throne and dreamed up by the Conservative party I suggest that this ministry will be responsible for reducing important services given to the people and not for improving the living conditions of small income citizens. However, that department has the responsibility to study thoroughy social programs of the federal and provincial governments such as the veterans pension, the old age security, the guaranteed income supplement, federal and provincial family allowances, tax credit for children, social welfare, social housing, school taxes, all those programs financed from taxes.
There are also programs paid by workers on top of their income tax, including the Canada Pension Plan, unemployment insurance, automobile insurance and work income supplement in Quebec and, in other provinces, private pension plans. There is also the Workmen's Compensation Board which is financed by companies. In fact, if we study all those programs to establish a guaranteed income policy allowing small income citizens to obtain higher allowances, I entirely agree.
Mr. Speaker, these days much is said about the proposed dismantling of Petro-Canada by selling stocks to Canadians. I believe that this decision is a real joke for small income citizens. What about older people who have only the old age security pension and the guaranteed income supplement? Single persons get only $325.95 a month and a couple $602.44 a month. What about people who depend on welfare-in Quebec a single person gets only $276 a month and a couple $439? What about people living on minimum wage who get only $3.47 an hour in Quebec, which adds up to $555.20 a month before taxes, not to mention the 700,000 unemployed who get from $480 to $550 a month? What do you think those citizens are going to do with two oil shares? Their first reaction will be to sell their shares to the rich, so they can eat. In a matter of months they will be the losers, because the new shareholders will ask the government to raise oil prices and subsidize their operations. Those will be the facts.
Mr. Speaker, there is a reference in the throne speech to parliamentary reform, and I quote:
You will also be asked to consider reforms to extend the power of Parliament. Proposals will be submitted to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization to strengthen the powers and resources of parliamentary committees, to accord more prominence to private members' initiatives, and to make my ministers more accountable to you. The standing committee also will be invited to consider the question of a permanent Speaker for the House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, how can I believe in those reforms to give more powers to members of Parliament? How can the Prime

October 17, 1979
The Address-Mr. Ferguson
Minister say such a thing, when he himself took powers away from his own members and even made "back-bencher" or second-class ministers by establishing an inner cabinet to control the whole cabinet? To quote from the press release issued by the Prime Minister's Office:
Mr. Clark has announced that the reorganization of cabinet included the establishment of a main cabinet committee overseeing five policy sub-committees. The major policies of government will be developed mainly by that group.
And we note the absence of ministers to represent the majority of the people.
The main cabinet committee, chaired by the Prime Minister, will develop government priorities and take decisions on major policy aspects stemming from those priorities.
Now, Mr. Speaker, here are two documents both signed by the government, two documents which contradict one another. That is why I am anxious to see that reform. To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I believe that if we are to improve the standard of living for people with low income, who are always the first to be affected by any increase in the cost of living, we will have, first, to prevent any further increase in oil prices; second, establish a policy to give subsidies to tenants; third, maintain and improve Canada Works and Young Canada Works programs; fourth, review all CMHC's programs; fifth, stop all cuts in unemployment benefits; sixth, study the possibility of allowing any citizen to retire and get old age benefits at the age of 60; and, seventh, establish a guaranteed minimum income plan.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to participate in the throne speech debate in this the first session of the Thirty-first Parliament of Canada. I wish to congratulate you, sir, on your election as Speaker of this House. Your fairness and skill in carrying out your duties are well known across Canada.
Furthermore, I am delighted to congratulate the mover and seconder to the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. Both the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz) and the hon. member for Cardigan (Mr. MacDonald) displayed a concern for their constituencies and for Canada which, I hope, will set the tone for this session of Parliament. I would also like to congratulate the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Clark) for his success on May 22. I am pleased to be part of this new government.
I have come to this House of Commons with a record of nearly 28 years of service to the public, Yb'h years with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and four years as police chief for the city of Saint John, New Brunswick. Both careers were very satisfying to me. In many ways the Royal Canadian Mounted Police represents Canada to the rest of the world. My pride in being a member of that force remains undiminished and untarnished.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It is also a particular source of pride to me to be the first police chief of a major Canadian city to be elected to the House of Commons of Canada.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Saint John, New Brunswick, has one of the oldest police forces in North America. It has the oldest police union in the world, having been organized in 1918. Unrest in municipal police departments captures headlines in the newspapers much too often. The reasons are much too complex to describe at this time. In my present role as a member of Parliament it is my fondest wish to use my knowledge in police work to alleviate some of the problems.
As a member of the Canadian Association of Police Chiefs I was cognizant of the fact that resolutions received by the previous federal government were not given the attention they deserved. If in some way I, as a member of Parliament, can serve as a catalyst between the federal government and the police community, then I believe I will have served well.
I wish to thank the people of Saint John for having elected me. I hope I can maintain their confidence during my years in the House of Commons and serve my city and country to the best of my ability.
Mr. Speaker, I have come to Parliament to speak for the city of Saint John. I have come to speak for the factory workers, the drydock workers, for the office workers, for senior citizens and young people, for sailors and fishermen, for business and labour. Indeed, I have come to work for every citizen in the city of Saint John, and to work for Canada. I have come to speak, not with a noose in my back pocket or with a narcotic control act in my right hand, but, rather, I have come here with compassion and concern, a belief that things can be better, that we as members must do better, and I am prepared to work as hard as I am able to aid this government in bringing about necessary changes.
These necessary changes are ones which will improve the quality of life. We need, for example, to inquire into the needs of the disabled and handicapped, to strengthen the role of the voluntary sector, to extend spouses' allowances in certain circumstances, and to amend certain legislation respecting veterans. These are just a few of the programs to be considered as a means of improving life for Canadians. More will be brought in, more will be approved. More are required.
During the past five years Saint John, New Brunswick, has been the only city in Atlantic Canada where there has been a reduction in the number of federal government jobs. Indeed, in that period there has been no growth at all. In fact there has been a decrease. The previous federal government, starting in 1975, had set in motion a program designed to bankrupt the city in terms of federal positions. Thirty-seven jobs from the Department of Veterans Affairs are moving to Halifax, 77 jobs from Revenue Canada are going to St. John's, Newfoundland, and five positions in the Post Office Department are going to Halifax. I realize that this program had been set in
October 17, 1979

motion by the previous government between three and five years ago. To my mind it has been a bad decision. I have met with the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Baker) and the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. McKinnon). 1 have met with the Minister of State (Transport) (Mr. Howie). Mr. Speaker, if nothing can be done about the program at this stage, I ask that steps be taken to compensate for the loss of these 119 jobs. During the recent campaign I attacked the previous administration for implementing this program. The people of Saint John are now looking to me for action.
The city of Saint John bid for the 1977 summer games. The federal government of the day appointed a three-member independent sports committee to inspect the various sites in respect of which application had been made for the games. This committee gave its unqualified support to Saint John, New Brunswick. The then mayor of Saint John, Mr. Robert Lockhart, the city council and Mr. Ev. Trites, chairman of the steering committee, worked very hard, along with other members of the committee, and Saint John itself spent in excess of $60,000 putting forward a presentation which had full support from the province of New Brunswick. But in the infinite wisdom of the previous administration, a political decision was made and announced, contrary to the recommendation of the independent study. The hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Lalonde), who was then the minister responsible, made this political announcement. Mr. Speaker, the citizens of Saint John had worked their hearts out to get these games and they were all bitterly disappointed.
In 1985 Saint John will be celebrating its 200th birthday. In the same year New Brunswick has been designated to hold the summer games. To my mind there are many reasons for the games to be held in Saint John this time around, but the overriding reasons must be as follows: first, we want them in Saint John; second, the city and council have voted 100 per cent to have them there and are prepared to put up their share of the money; third, the games will provoke an unparalleled degree of community spirit which will do wonders for the city and, fourth, they will provide much-needed structures which will be of lasting benefit to the people. It will be an honour for us to welcome athletes from across the country who come to take part in the summer games of 1985. All these reasons are tremendously valid, but the overriding reasons for bringing the games to Saint John is because it will be our 200th birthday.
The Saint John harbour toll bridge in the centre of our city is a federal structure which has been plunging deeper and deeper into debt each year. This bridge was completed in September, 1968, at a cost of $18 million, and the interest on the debt in 1978 was $1.2 million. The cost of maintenance and expenses for the same year amounted to $600,000. The income from tolls in 1978 amounted to $1.3 million, leaving a net loss for the last operating year of $500,000. The total debt to date is now $26.8 million and rising.
1 should like to quote from a report to the House of Commons by the Auditor General, Mr. J. J. Macdonell, on March 31, 1977:
The Address-Mr. Ferguson
Revenues of the Saint John harbour bridge have been insufficient to meet principal and interest payments on the National Harbours Board loan and the advance from the Municipal Development and Loan Board. The miscellaneous loan from the Department of Finance was made to cover the shortfalls on repayments of principal and interest. In these circumstances, these loans cannot be regarded as fully collectible.
The province of New Brunswick has offered to assume the maintenance costs of the bridge provided a transfer of ownership occurs and the debt is forgiven. The bridge would then become an integral part of the provincial highway system. 1 would appeal the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) to forgive this debt and proceed with the transfer of ownership as soon as possible.
The port of Saint John has seen great growth in the past decade and hopes to double the present tonnage by the year 1990. I would like to express my gratitude to the hon. Richard B. Hatfield, Premier of New Brunswick, for his government's involvement in the construction of the Rodney terminal container pier. This is the only instance in Canadian history of a provincial government providing economic and political leadership in an area which is truly a federal responsibility. Had it not been for this involvement in the amount of $25 million, Saint John would surely have become a secondary port on the eastern seaboard. Indeed, we would not now be in the container business at all.
We in Saint John were pleased with the announcement by the Minister of State for Transport last June concerning a contract in excess of $13 million for port development. This expansion was very much needed and will allow our port to handle more goods more efficiently. Much more is required. With the development of great potash mines in the Sussex area only 50 miles from Saint John, terminal facilities are now required to handle the additional tonnage. The port of Saint John has an excellent labour force. We want to handle additional cargo, and I am sure the shippers we serve will be well satisfied with our performance.
My background dictates that I be concerned with the protection of human life. The time has long passed for a close investigation to be carried out not only in the port of Saint John but in every port across Canada to ensure that the safety of the workers is paramount. Too many deaths and serious injuries have taken place which could have been prevented had proper safeguards and security measures been implemented.
We have in the city of Saint John one of the best shipyards in Canada, if not the best. At the present time the yards employ in the vicinity of 1,800 people. The Saint John Dry-dock and Shipbuilding Company has the labour force, and the expertise which is required to ensure that Canada takes its rightful place in the world of super vessels. As set out in the throne speech, the Clark government will ensure an even flow of work to Canadian shipyards. This is the type of government program we welcome and encourage, one which builds on the strength of a region and promotes stability in our economy.
In order for Saint John Drydock and Shipbuilding to construct super vessels and carry out ship repairs which meet the

October 17, 1979
The Address-Mr. Ferguson
standards of world demand, it is necessary to undertake expansion of existing facilities. We are looking to the Department of Regional Economic Expansion to aid us in this goal.
We in Saint John and Atlantic Canada have a real contribution to make to Canada and to confederation. We are blessed with a wealth of natural resources and resourceful talent. Atlantic Canada is strong. We have a fine history in shipbuilding, farming, forestry, mining and fishing. We have great sea ports, beautiful beaches, and unpolluted streams. We are a good people, and that is really our strength. We look to the federal government in Saint John and in the Atlantic region for leadership and encouragement to build upon our strengths. We look to the federal government for incentives to improve our economy and lifestyle.
It is important that collectively our citizens, business, labour, and government at all levels, work hand in hand to develop our area and to make opportunities available in order that our young people can stay at home if they so choose and take their rightful place in society.
The opportunities to develop a wide range of energy resources in Atlantic Canada are unparalleled. There is great opportunity to develop our coal reserves and to explore the concept of harnessing the beautiful Bay of Fundy tides, including wave energy. It is now for us to move with haste in development and research in this regard.
On the outskirts of Saint John there is Point Lepreau, a nuclear plant which is programmed to go into operation within the next 18 months. As in most areas in the country, in Saint John there is much concern about safety. 1 am pleased that this government will be setting up a parliamentary committee to study all aspects of nuclear power. For Canada today nuclear power is becoming one alternative to conventional fossil fuels. Safety at all times has to be the overriding concern.
1 am pleased that the government will form a youth employment secretariat. This will streamline all the federal programs under one department. Young people must have the opportunity to work and grow in this country. If the economic climate continues to affect young people from across the country adversely, we will sow seeds of disillusionment rather than seeds of hope. Every effort must be made to encourage job training and retraining for young people. This is mandatory in an ever-changing society.
In excess of 51 per cent of the people of this country are female. 1 am pleased that this government will place before parliament an employment strategy for women. Today only 3.5 per cent of the membership of the House of Commons are women. Not only have women been missing in significant numbers from the House of Commons, but they have also been missing from boardrooms, commissions, and the policy-making areas of our political system.

We in Saint John and all those from one end of this country to the other have the natural resources and the will to accomplish this goal.
