Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to congratulate you and your assistant on you appointments to these most important posts in the House. As this is my maiden speech, 1 should like to say something about my riding.
For a number of reasons I am proud to represent the Laurier constituency on Montreal Island. First of all, it is quite a privilege to sit as a member in the House of Commons, the highest legislative body in Canada. My constituency, named after the eighth Prime Minister of Canada, has been represented in the past by a long list of imposing personalities. For instance, it was ably represented during the last Parliament as well as the past 15 years by the hon. Fernand Leblanc, who has been appointed to the Senate. Senator Leblanc, like all those who had preceded him in the House, had always been close to his constituents. As a matter of fact, the people of this riding have always been privileged ever since it became a constituency in 1935. Their first representative was the Hon. E. Bertrand, a minister in the St. Laurent cabinet. After his appointment to the bench, he was replaced by the Hon. J. Eugene Lefran$ois, later appointed to the Senate, Its next representative was the Hon. Lionel Chevrier, a minister of transport in the Mackenzie King and St. Laurent governments, and both a minister of justice and solicitor general in the Pearson government. He was later appointed High Commissioner to London.
All those men served their country loyally and constantly. For the benefit of hon. members, 1 shall explain the geographic and demographic situation of the riding of Laurier. Located east of downtown Montreal, it extends from Park Avenue in the west to Papineau to the east, from Sherbrooke in the south to Bernard St. and the railway track in the north. Amongst its better known streets let us mention Laurier, St. Joseph, Parc La Fontaine, the commercial street, Mont-Royal, St. Denis, St. Louis Square and St. Laurent or the "Main", where traditionally east Montreal joins west Montreal. The population of the riding is 65 per cent Francophone and comprises several minorities of which the main one, numerically, is Portuguese. It also includes considerable numbers of Canadians of various origins: English, Greek, Spanish, Italian, Chinese and eastern European. In fact, every corner of the world is represented in the riding.
The Address-Mr. Berger
The riding has been and still is one of the areas where one of the larger numbers of immigrants settle; to my mind, it truly represents the Canadian mosaic. Some time ago, the riding had a fairly large number of Jewish people who were immortalized in the writings of Mordecai Richler. Before going any further, Mr. Speaker, I should like to express all my gratitude to the people of the riding of Laurier for welcoming me so warmly as a candidate, and electing me with quite a large majority. I hope I shall prove worthy of the trust the riding has put in me.
Mr. Speaker, as a candidate taking his first few steps in the field of politics, I have noticed a mood of impatience amongst my electors, impatience with the governments at every level which take so long to find solutions to their problems. As an example of what I mean, 1 should like to describe the housing situation in my riding. Since the election 1 have received a great number of calls from people in their sixties who, after working for 40 years, want to move into low rental housing. These are often sick people who live in those three storey houses with outside staircases, typical of eastern Montreal. They can barely keep up their homes which are often badly heated. There is a lack of low rental housing in Montreal, as was noted in a newspaper article last spring, which stated that there were 9,000 such units which were occupied, with a waiting list of over 11,000.
A related problem is the shabbiness of these houses in general in my riding. The Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation has a residential rehabilitation assistance program administered by the city of Montreal. The need for such a program is self-evident because our downtown areas are in dire need of renovation. However the problems that I have noted in the implementation of this program put its adequacy in question.
Some low-income tenants-some of whom have been living in the same apartment for over 30 years while others are ill and even often handicapped-have been advised that their lease will be cancelled at some future date when government approval is obtained. The owners are unable to set the rental rates before undertaking the construction. The tenants doubt that the projects will ever be undertaken but feel that the owners will rather make some superficial repairs to take advantage of government subsidies at their expense. Tenants' associations have been set up to fight against those projects or suggest some alternatives.
Mr. Speaker, when tenants move and buildings become half empty, the services worsen. The owners say that present subsidies are not high enough to meet ever soaring construction costs, with the concrete result that rents are higher after repairs and this prevents some low-income tenants from moving back into their apartment. No step has been taken to relocate the tenants during construction. In addition, there is no co-ordination between that renewal program and provincial
318

October 17, 1979
The Address-Mr. Berger
legislation on rental which does not even allow owners to cancel leases to make repairs. Consequently the parties enter into endless legal proceedings which bring no adequate solution. I welcome the statement made by the Prime Minister last week in this debate when he said that his government would undertake to launch studies if that could lead to better solutions than those proposed by the government. 1 urge him and his minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to undertake a study on how this problem can be resolved as soon as possible and to refer that study to the appropriate House committee.
Mr. Speaker, unemployment is another major concern in my constituency. Not only are jobs needed, but the problem is even more far-reaching since we have to face structural unemployment. It seems to me that the young men and women graduating from high schools and community colleges do not have adequate education. They do not know how to find a job and they often have qualifications in fields where there is no job. I recall a few years ago 1 heard someone in the aviation industry say that his company badly needed aeronautical engineers. Unfortunately not one single student graduated from Quebec schools in that particular field that year. Cana-dair was faced with a similar problem; because of the success met by its Challenger operation in the last few years, it had to set up training programs for non-qualified labour.
Mr. Speaker, how could we fail to understand the growing impatience of a population faced with such permanent problems and unacceptable conditions such as the grain handlers strike in the port of Montreal, which has already been going on for five months, and a public transit strike which paralyses the whole city. If the Minister of Labour (Mr. Alexander) were here, I would ask him how long he intends to wait before taking measures to put an end to the strike affecting the port of Montreal. That question has been put on several occasions in this House. We all know that we live in a great country whose wealth in natural resources is unparalleled and we should ask ourselves why nothing is done to solve these problems.

Mr. Speaker, I am concerned about the new government. It says that it is committed to efficiency and to cutting out waste. Important steps in the process of reform were initiated in the last Parliament, as has been acknowledged by a Conservative minister. But I am afraid that for the sake of satisfying its doctrinaire philosophy the government will cut out good programs and dismiss competent personnel. It has already done so. We are now losing a considerable amount of the expertise which has been assembled in Ottawa in the past 16 years.
The Anti-Inflation Board, while often criticized, accomplished much for which it will receive a general recognition in the future. During the summer I read a publication of the Board entitled "Inflation and Economic Policy", which I believe was distributed to all members of the House. The authors of the report stressed the limitations of economic policy. Because

of the slowness of the economy to respond to monetary and fiscal stimulus, they favour a policy of gradual expansion. Selective measures, they said, should be used to correct weaknesses in the economy, for example, to fight structural unemployment, to which I referred earlier, and to develop particular industries. This government, with its doctrinaire philosophy, has ignored this advice. Rather than improving programs that were developed after much research and consultation with experts in many fields, it has wastefully committed $2 billion annually for a housing program that everyone knows is not a housing program.
Another important program which has suffered from budget cuts is the Canada Works program which provided employment and tangible social services to my riding and many others with high unemployment. I have received dozens of calls, from distressed older persons in particular, who benefited from this program in the past and are at a loss to make do in the months ahead. I urge the government to restore the program to its original levels. Unfortunately I feel my words and those of my colleagues fall on deaf ears.
We in Quebec have been preoccupied with the referendum. It is part of our daily lives. Bill 101 has been confusing for many English Canadians in Quebec and across Canada who have difficulty reconciling the apparent contradiction of a unilingual Quebec with a bilingual Canada. Initiatives by the Parti Quebecois to shift the burden of bilingualism, as they put it, and to give Quebec a French face, have created tensions and led to economic loss and hardship. Some aspects of Bill 101 are clearly excessive and will be changed by a Liberal government, but English Canadians must recognize the concern which French Canadians have for the survival of the French language, as well as the economic consequences that language has for French Canadians to this day.
Most Canadians rebel at the thought of legally obliging children to attend French schools, yet in many cases French Canadians have always been forced to learn English in order to earn a living, which in effect amounts to the same thing. Furthermore, no matter what language legislation is adopted, or even if Quebec achieves independence, any French Canadian who wishes to advance in many areas of human endeavour will have to learn English.
Perhaps no aspect of Liberal policy was more controversial and misunderstood than the previous government's efforts to create a sense of belonging to Canada for French Canadians, and yet no policy was more vital to the survival of our country. I must confess that I have great difficulty in understanding the begrudging manner in which some English Canadians greet the French presence in our country. I am proud of our two principal languages. On a trip to Cape Breton Island some years ago I was pleasantly surprised to find a number of French villages along the coast which, in spite of all obstacles, had managed to keep their language, culture, and character. The French language outside of Quebec is like a precious flower Canadians must cherish.
October 17, 1979

The right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Trudeau), in a speech to the Canadian Association of Broadcasters in Winnipeg in April, 1977, tried to explain the objectives of the government's language Policy. He said that sometimes he wished that the government had never described the official languages policy as "bilingualism", because the word apparently implied the intent that all Canadians learn two languages. Also he said:
Such is not our intent at all. What we have is simply a program for.. . greater equality between two languages, either one or the other of which is spoken by virtually every Canadian.
In trying to explain what language means to people he said:
Just as when you speak English, when a Quebecker speaks French it is something he does naturally and automatically-almost like breathing. That is precisely why language is so important: because when you limit a person's use of his language, it is almost like interfering with his breathing. When we cannot speak our own language, we feel stifled, a bit as if we are choking.
This speech was made several months after the election of the Parti Quebecois. Also our leader tried to explain why Quebeckers had voted as they did. He referred to the economic opportunities which had been denied to French Canadians in private industry. He tried to explain why the air traffic controllers dispute had become such a potent symbol to Quebeckers. He said that he felt it was in large part because the most visibly modern, future-oriented job sector of aviation seemed to be saying to Quebeckers that the tasks, in which other people all over the world are normally able to use their own language, are ones in which they may never look forward to using the French language in Quebec.
He stated that in Quebec the private sector would have to provide more opportunity for French Canadians to work hard and make decent progress using the French language only. On the national level, corporate business and other private organizations would have to make room for and share more power with the French Canadian who speaks English. Provincial and municipal governments would have to offer more administrative and educational services in French in areas where there were important French-speaking minorities. The federal government was quite willing to share costs in this respect. Our leader concluded by saying that our country could remain united only if French Canadians wished to and were able to participate fully in Canadian society.
It is evident that Mrs. Stephenson, the minister of education of Ontario, has not listened to these important words in refusing to establish a separate French school in Penetangui-shene because of the cost. Also it is evident that some of those industries which have left Quebec in the last several years did not hear these words or did not care to hear them. In the final analysis they have done a great disservice to our country.
Just last week Canada's Commissioner of Official Languages remarked that Canada must become a comfortable and acceptable homeland for French-speaking Canadians or the country will not survive. Mr. Yalden said:
Language reform is not an option for Canada, it is a basic requirement. Without it there will be no Canada, at least not as we have known it.
The Address-Mr. Berger
Notwithstanding the substantial efforts made by my leader and his government, we face today the greatest crisis in our history. It is a crisis which concerns all Canadians, not just those living in Quebec. In his remarks in this debate last week, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) stated that it was the duty of all members of this House to speak to the people of Quebec about a strong Canada and about maintaining our confederation. With all due respect, I believe that that duty extends to the rest of Canada as well. Each and every member of this House has the duty to explain the reality of this country to his constituents because, in the final analysis, as the Pepin-Robarts commission stated, it is only through a change in attitudes on the part of all Canadians that we will solve our national unity crisis. I have felt for some time that it is only through accommodation, generosity, vision, and will on the part of all Canadians, that Canada will survive and prosper.
But as our leader has pointed out, it seems that our language problem may be only one manifestation of a greater problem, a crisis of our national will. We are witnessing today the balkanization of our country where there is no national interest, just the interests of the provinces. The arguments of our leader are lightly dismissed as having no practical application by those scrambling aboard the bandwagon of decentralization. When our leader was prime minister he was often accused of being insensitive to the demands of certain parts of the country, and of seeing matters in only one light. I agree with the opinion expressed by a member of the government party last week when he said that the people of western Canada had judged our leader very harshly and that history will judge him with greater kindness and greater objectivity.
This country is not as easy to manage as the present government believed when it was in opposition. The solutions are not straightforward as they are now finding. I urge the right hon. Prime Minister not to dismiss the warnings of our leader out of hand. There are many, many Canadians who are now starting to ask, "What chance does Canada have?"
For those who feel that national interest has no practical application, I should like to remind the House of the impediments to the free movement of capital and labour which have been established in our country in recent years. During my election campaign I met a number of construction workers in my riding who were accustomed to working in Ontario when the industry was slow in Quebec. Thanks to the construction war between the two provinces they can no longer do so. I believe that is an area which falls within the domain of the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Alexander), and I would ask him to undertake everything possible to attempt to ensure that we restore the free movement of labour for the benefit of all Canadian workers.
If I may, I should like to suggest a policy which could provide inestimable benefits for the whole of Canada. Every Canadian knows that the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway was a vital element in establishing a country from coast to coast. It was essential to provide a cheap efficient system of transportation. The world today is struggling with the problem of providing sufficient energy for its needs while

October 17, 1979
The Address-Mr. Berger
Canada is struggling to compete in world markets. In spite of our vast energy resources we are not divorced from this problem, as the hon. Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn) has found out in recent weeks and months.
Perhaps the profits from our energy resources should be devoted to developing a system of high speed intercity rail passenger transportation which would conserve energy and provide employment. Investment in such high technology areas would certainly reap dividends in exports as well. I believe Canada's subsidies for uneconomic passenger services for 1977 amounted to approximately $196 million. The United States will spend $800 million in fiscal 1979 in subsidies to Amtrack. For those people who think that is enough for a country of that size, I should like to point out the figures I have of subsidies for intercity rail passenger services in European countries and Japan. Britain spent $700 million in 1978, France spent $900 million, Italy spent $1.5 billion, and Japan spent $4.1 billion. Is it any wonder that North Americans, and more particularly Canadians, are the highest per capita users of energy in the world?
I, and others in this House, represent a generation of Canadians who grew up in the 1960s. We have heard for years and years of the greatness of Canada, about its potential, its people, its rich resources, its oceans, its farmlands and its cities. I would like to think that 1 might be able to say to this House on behalf of my generation that we feel it is time to act.
A Liberal colleague, the hon. member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Flis), stated earlier in the week that it was embarrassing to have to admit to foreigners that our constitution is still in England. I agree with that feeling. It is time we patriated our constitution. It is time it was amended to give the provinces what is rightfully theirs, but also to provide for the national interest. We must put these matters behind us so that we can begin to realize our potential. We want leadership from this House and from our governments. I for one do not want to be sitting here 15 years from now rehashing the same arguments we have heard for the last ten years, especially on this side of the House.
In spite of the differences of opinion among the members of this House, we share a belief in the future of Canada. Sometimes we will have occasion to be discouraged, but that should not diminish our purpose. Some time ago I read a statement by Walter Cronkite which perhaps indicates why I am in this House today. I am sure that similar motives have spurred other members of this House, and I should like to read this. When asked what he would tell kids getting out of school today in an age when a diploma no longer has the clout it had, he said:
I tell them . .. that the challenges are so immense that it's an absolute crime and a sin not to get involved in attempting to meet these challenges, and to try to find solutions to the problems .. . one could be justifiably pessimistic about the state of the world and the survival of man ... (kids) can become very cynical. They can say, "Why fight it, let me get mine in any way I can", or drop out-but not fight the problems. But they've got to fight the problems and it should be a great adventure to fight the problems-that's what I try to tell them. It ought to be great to get out there and see if you can make the thing work.
[Mr. Berger.J
Let us face these challenges with confidence and resolve, Mr. Speaker. Thank you.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Kilgour (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, permit me, sir, to express the pride I feel at being a small part of the new government and to participate here as the new member of Parliament for Edmonton-Strathcona. With others here I have an opportunity not only to bring the concerns of my constituents to this body, but I hope as well to bring a little youthful idealism to some national issues.
Last week the opinion was expressed by an hon. member opposite that the Conservatives are so busy preaching what is right, they have forgotten what is good. I cannot accept, sir, the separation of that which is right from that which is good. This common sense principle has not, unfortunately, been applied in the governing of this country during the past years. The consequences of not having done so have been serious and have left the new government a legacy of urgent and threatening problems, problems which affect us not only as individual citizens, but as members of a free and democratic society.
The difficulties Canada faces today cannot, of course, be laid solely at the feet of past leadership. We are caught, along with the rest of the world, in the dilemmas of modern man. Ours is an age characterized by dissolution of tradition and old values. Ours is an age of unlimited expectation and increasingly limited means. Most crucially, we are in an age when it is not uncommon for those who govern, for those who administer the rules, to have lost faith in their own legitimacy.
Little wonder, then, that citizens question the legitimacy of rules. It is for this very reason, namely, to re-establish the trust and belief in the legitimacy of government, that the basis of governmental decision making must be rooted in what we believe is right rather than that which is merely expedient under the circumstances.
What is at stake in this kind of decision making is not Progressive Conservatism or Liberalism, or any other "party-ism", but the ability to think clearly about what can and cannot be done to resolve the problems Canada faces today.
The most imminent of such problems is the presence of chronic inflation, in my opinion, and I think in the opinion of the vast majority of my constituents, at least; inflation which wipes out savings, impoverishes pensioners, rewards speculators, punishes many hard-working citizens, discourages private investment and productivity, and hinders trade competitiveness.
Helmut Schmidt, Chancellor of West Germany, has said that "inflation for economies is a killer disease". The symptoms of this disease are manifest both in a nation as a whole and in the workings of government. Inflation has also taken a toll on national morality. Witness the recklessness of consumer buying, the underlying insecurity, the loosening of responsibility at all levels of society, and the growing lack of respect for older pillars of society, including parents.
The symptoms of inflation are evident in our government's reluctant acceptance of three recent hikes in the bank rate of
October 17, 1979

the Bank of Canada, raises increasingly damaging to the ordinary citizen, homeowner, farmer, and businessman alike.
The fact is, sir, in my opinion, that we are presently reacting to a situation created during the past six or seven years during which time our federal government spent more than it raised, financed its debts on credit, and intentionally inflated the supply of paper dollars. In an effort to do good, to meet the pleas in favour of social betterment, the previous government provided a lot of bad examples to Canadians.
Our major economic problems today stem in large measure, sir, from the inflationary bias of past government policies, policies which motivated citizens to spend too much and to save too little. Federal taxes, the budget and monetary policies all promoted immediate consumption instead of investment for the future. The result has been a less productive work force, a reduction in real growth, and an upswing in expectations. The reason has been too much money chasing too few goods.
From 1968 to 1978 the Canadian money supply, as defined by "Ml", increased by approximately 160 per cent. During this time real economic growth in our country was about 54 per cent. The general price level in the economy increased by 106 per cent, a percentage very close to the amount of new money printed in a vain attempt to prime the pump or spur the economy.
One has to ask, I think on all sides of the Flouse, why the previous government permitted the money supply growth to reach the point where the governor of the Bank of Canada now must talk about braking? A most important reason, of course, was the need to finance the rising federal debt brought on by deficit after deficit. Deficits can hardly be blamed on the Bank of Canada. In the period from 1968 to 1978 federal spending nearly quintupled.
Americans are worried about their current deficit of $30 billion, yet proportionately our current deficit is nearly three times the size. In U.S. terms the Canadian deficit would be more than $110 billion.
After the election, approximately 39 per cent of persons interviewed by Gallup pollsters indicated they considered rising prices or inflation to be Canada's number one problem. Our deficit is too high and the reduction of that deficit is one of the government's main tasks. Our government is pledged to curb government spending, but it will take real toughness to bring that deficit under control. Inflation must be attacked at its root cause. Not only must there be a cutback in deficit spending, excessive expansion of the monetary base must be stopped.
Being a lawyer, I believe in consulting precedents, especially when those precedents are impressive. West Germany is a country with a rock solid economy. During 1978, West Germany had a trade surplus of $21 billion. Its GNP is expected to grow more than 4.5 per cent in 1979. Inflation is not expected to exceed 4 per cent. Helmut Schmidt believes that the first among the greatest world problems is the notion-I am paraphrasing-to consume more than is produced and to
The Address-Mr. Kilgour fill in the gap by printing money. I believe we should heed Chancellor Schmidt's advice. The opinion of Mr. Schmidt is already shared by a number of economists both in the United States and Canada.
The solutions they propose include the following measures: first, consistent policies of moderate monetary growth; second, long-term tax incentives to encourage saving and investment; third, working toward balancing the budget and discouraging excessive consumer spending; fourth, reduction in government spending; fifth, the scrapping of destructive and wasteful government regulations, and sixth, a reduction of the government's over-all role in the economy in order to encourage personal incentive and private sector competition. The direction of the new government as revealed in the throne speech is very much in the direction of these proposals.
Like others in this House on all sides, I suspect, 1 am perplexed by the latest bank rate increase. It has given Canadians the highest real cost of borrowing in Canadian history-much higher than in the United States because inflation in that country is now running at about 14 per cent compared to about 9 per cent in this country. 1 am aware that the United States must try to keep its nominal interest rates above its inflation rate. But if inflation in that country goes to, say, 30 per cent because of bad fiscal, energy, and monetary policy in Washington, must this mean that the bank rate in Canada will automatically go 33 per cent or 34 per cent as well?
I realize that our central bank defends such increases as being necessary to maintain the value of our dollar in foreign exchange markets. But surely the difference in our current inflation rates must inevitably cause our dollar to move upward relative to the United States dollar. As for our balance of payments problem as a whole, I am persuaded that there are now probably more basic cures than monetary ones, such as exporting some of our surplus natural gas, moving more export grain, etc.
In short, Mr. Speaker, I believe that inflation has completely destroyed the credibility of the previous government, as well as the value of Canadian dollars. Borrowing by the government in the past has primarily been to hide an inept economic performance, and intentionally to keep the fly wheel of inflation turning. There we can vividly see an example of where expediency took precedence over right. The new government has an enormous task ahead of it. It will take a great effort, and courage, to curb expenditures. Nevertheless, this task is a vital one. Otmar Emminger, head of West Germany's equivalent of the United States Federal Reserve, has said that "inflation is like a dictator-it must be fought before it becomes established, or it is too late".
Next to the state of the economy the most serious concern of the people in Edmonton-Strathcona appears to me to be the growing violent crime rate in the west, and in Edmonton in particular. The 1977 Statistics Canada figures indicate that Edmonton had more violent crimes than any other major Canadian city. The violent crime rate per capita was more than double the average for Canada as a whole. From 1977 to

October 17, 1979
The Address-Mr. Kilgour
1978, for instance, murders in Edmonton increased by fully 85 per cent.
The increase in crime is also apparent in the whole Canadian context, evident in the national crime rate, which has gone up about 152 per cent during the last sixteen-year period, with crimes of violence approximately doubling. The disturbing fact is that crime rates have been rapidly going up in a period when Canadians have been enjoying both rapidly improving living standards and social services. How can this be explained?
Charles E. Silberman, author of "Criminal Violence, Criminal Justice", a fairly recently published work, notes that most crime is committed by people between the ages of 14 and 25 years of age. Silberman believes many of these adolescents are committing crimes because of the weakening of adult social controls.
I noted before that we live in an age where the old values are being questioned. This is equally true of our criminal justice system. After all, our justice system reflects the predominant social values of the day. The criminal law was originally fashioned with the idea that citizens entered into the social contract with the understanding that society would guarantee, or at least put a premium on, their lives, dignity, and right to possessions. Especially during the past decade our criminal justice system changed its emphasis from that of reform to that of rehabilitation, based on social scientists' convictions that most crime is rooted in environmental causes. The concept of rehabilitation has undeniably proved to be a failure. By the 1970s it had become clear that prisons were not effectively rehabilitating prisoners. The same faces were appearing in front of the courts with startling regularity.
It has also become clear that present parole laws have not been very effective. A 1974 study of penitentiary parole by the solicitor general's office showed that 53.7 per cent of the individuals released were back in prison within five years of their release.
I believe I am justified in saying that there is a growing conviction in the country that the mild treatment of convicted violent criminals, and I would stress "violent", has contributed to soaring crime rates. More important, there is an increasing fear of criminals by the citizens of this country, a fear that is gradually turning into real resentment.
A society in which crime goes without real punishment and victims receive no justice for their injury is a society that may turn to vigilante justice. Witness the increasing numbers of Canadians inclined to favour capital punishment.
Our criminal justice system constitutes a key element of our social fabric. It follows, in my opinion, that people will act, to some extent, according to how they believe society views their actions. A sentence not commensurate with the gravity of the crime indicates to the violent offender that his action is not regarded by society as a serious breach of social norms. Would not criminals be more effectively deterred by raising the penalties involved in violent crime as well as raising the opportunities and rewards offered by a non-criminal existence?

Cynicism and indifference to good and evil are products of a society that is less concerned with the needs of those who observe its rules than with those who break them. Guidance respecting acceptable social behaviour must be provided in our social structure, especially for the young members of our society. The starting point for this, of course, should be the family and the educational system. These institutions must be reinforced by our justice system, through measures that, first, provide sentences commensurate with the severity of violent crimes; second, distinguish between the professional criminal and the occasional offender; and third, implement common sense rules with respect to parole and bail.
[ Translation]
The last point I wish to bring to the attention of the House is the constitutional matter. The Quebec referendum, coming along with the recent provincial disagreements, will give great urgency to the problems related to the nature of Canadian federalism, as it is described in our constitution. The last century has obviously brought drastic changes to the structure of Canada. The growth of technological innovation as well as the growing diversity within Canada have required changes to the role of governments. These changes have been accompanied by growing confusion over the relations between the national and provincial governments.
Many Canadians, particularly in western Canada and in Quebec, have considered the policies of the previous regime to be harmful to the true federal system. The impact of these policies indicates that a number of citizens regard Ottawa as monolithic and insensitive to provincial needs, contrary to the spirit of the British North America Act.
It is becoming even more obvious that the provinces are little inclined to melt into a unitary and centralized state like France or Great Britain. The provinces believe that under such conditions the value of the language, the cultural traditions and their respective economic environment, which vary from one province to another, could become sources of frictions and debates. Also they think that it could be very harmful for our national unity.
The centralist point of view of Canada which considers the provinces as creations of the Canadian Parliament has indeed been refuted by the judiciary committee of the Privy Council since 1892 when it rejected the centralist argument in the case of the Maritime Bank, by upholding the intent behind the British North America Act which was neither to weld all the provinces together into one single state nor to subordinate the provincial governments under a central authority.
A country as large as Canada cannot be governed by and from Ottawa alone. If it were not a federal system, like a ten-link chain, it would be disunited. The Canadian economy cannot be designed to feed central Canada. A chain can be strong only if its links themselves are strong.
As for Quebec, it is imperative that there be significant resolve at the provincial level. Because of its cultural and
October 17, 1979

linguistic make-up, Quebec has need of a strong judicial and political structure to protect its interests and remain part of Canada. Few Quebeckers think that the changes in the constitution suggested by the former government were in fact based on the wish to protect provincial rights, when in fact nothing was done by that government in the last eight years to better the constitutional position of the provinces within confederation.
Whatever past errors may have been, time has come for all Canadians to express their devotion to Quebec. Canada and Quebec have need of one another if Canadians want to continue proving that citizens of various cultures and origins can build a country worthy of the envy of the whole wide world. Tearing it apart now, as the former prime minister said, would be "a sin against humanity". It is very easy for us, Canadians, who feel the same way, to recognize the need for such changes as will achieve a realistic balance between the provincial and federal governments.
In considering the changes in the constitution that would help national unity, attention could be concentrated on the following factors:	regional disparities, Senate reform,
entrenching the Supreme Court in the constitution, federal government purchasing power, entrenching the Canadian Bill of Rights. The new Clark government recognizes that a truly federal system demands that there be consultations between the responsible governments through federal-provincial conferences. In addition, it recognizes that the provinces must have a broad enough base on which to set up efficiently the institutional and economic foundation of their own economies with a view to meeting their development need better.
I have mentioned briefly three problem areas which, if not checked, could constitute a very real threat to the fundamental principles of our society.
The dilemma we face, as far as inflation is concerned, is that the methods used by the previous government to resolve tensions in the economy are the very methods which are most likely to undermine the foundations of our social system. In my opinion they have, to a substantial degree, destroyed our trust in money itself, the instrument of exchange through which we conduct all of our economic affairs.
It was Abraham Lincoln who said, "You can't bring about prosperity by discouraging thrift... You cannot help the wage-earner by pulling down the wage-payer ... You cannot establish sound security on borrowed money ... You cannot build character and courage by taking away man's initiative and independence. You cannot help men permanently by doing for them what they could do for themselves."
Second, with respect to the problem of crime, we must remember that law and order are a matter of civilization. When there is no proper control over crime, a proper social
The Address-Mr. Penner
order simply cannot be maintained. Thus crime threatens the social order in much the same way as does totalitarianism.
Criminal law in itself can never bring about a good society. However, it helps provide the framework within which a society can function.
Finally, with regard to the constitution, it must be remembered that in its expressive sense the constitution is a communication from the people to their governors of how they have asserted their freedoms and responsibilities. The federal government must be sensitive to this true spirit of our constitution and acknowledge its partnership role with the provinces in the governing of the nation.
The answers to the above problems have no easy solutions. There are no promising new doctrines or panaceas; there are only difficult and perhaps unpleasant choices. The root causes of these problems cannot be dealt with by experts or by abstract theories. They must be tackled by common sense people from a commonsense perspective that to effect something good one must proceed on the basis of what is right. This government, as the representative of the Canadian people, has the primary responsibility to proceed from the right to the good.
With the serious danger of chronic inflation, growing crime, and the threat to national unity, Canadians and the new government must recognize that this is a time for strength, a time for good will, a time for understanding and determination on all of our parts.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate I want to join with many others in congratulating the two new members of Parliament who moved and seconded the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. I agree with other hon. members that the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz) and the hon. member for Cardigan (Mr. MacDonald) performed well, and I know that their constituents will be extremely proud of them. All members in this House on the opening day of Parliament, that day of tradition, were pulling for these new members. We wanted them to do well, and they certainly did not fail us.
I want to say how pleased I am as a member of Parliament from northern Ontario that one of ours, the hon. member for Sudbury (Mr. Jerome), is once again the occupant of the Speaker's chair. It was my privilege to be associated with Mr. Speaker for one year during the Thirtieth Parliament in the capacity of deputy chairman of the whole House. That experience for me was not only enjoyable in every respect, but also it was an excellent opportunity to learn more about the intricacies of the procedures in this House, those mysteries of which the gentlemen at the Table know all, and when we go to them, will reveal to us what we need to know. During that year of working with Mr. Speaker I came to respect his quick mind and to appreciate his many talents and abilities.
I am now entering my twelth year as a member of this great democratic institution, the federal Parliament of Canada.

October 17, 1979
The Address-Mr. Penner Mr. Alexander: The class of '68.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Alexander) says the class of 68. That, of course, is not a very long period of service compared to some, but 1 can say to the new members of Parliament in this House that those nearly dozen years have gone by like an instant. So full, so demanding, and so challenging has the life and work of being a member of Parliament been, that time quite literally does fly.
A cynical friend of mine once said that one should never take up an occupation, profession or career that you enjoy too much because, if you do, you will find that it makes your life pass too quickly. My cynical friend would be ill-advised ever to enter active politics or become involved in public life, because he would discover that one's life does indeed pass by quickly. Weeks become like days, and years are often like months.
When I was called upon to speak a few minutes ago, I was identified by you, Mr. Speaker, as the member for Cochrane. That identification is still somewhat new to me, because for over a decade in this House, I was the member of Parliament for Thunder Bay. I should briefly explain that the old constituency of Thunder Bay was a large rural riding in northern Ontario. It was entirely rural, and included no part of what is now the city of Thunder Bay. That is all a little bit confusing.
To compress the story, boundaries were changed through the process of redistribution, and much could be said about how badly that was handled in the province of Ontario. I do not know about other provinces, but in my province it was done in a less than satisfactory manner. At any rate, as a result of that process, one third of the old Thunder Bay riding was joined with three quarters of the previous Cochrane riding to create what I call the new constituency of Cochrane.
No member of Parliament could ask for a better riding to represent in the Parliament of Canada. There may be, and I am sure there are, some that are as good, but there can be none better than the constituency of Cochrane. There are, for example, in the constituency of Cochrane French-speaking Canadians, English-speaking Canadians, new Canadians from all over the globe, and native Canadians, the original Canadians, and they live together in this part of northern Ontario in relative harmony and in an atmosphere of good will. The many differences among us are not merely tolerated, they are in fact respected.
The people of Cochrane are strong minded. They live in a developing region of this country, a resource rich region. What takes them there indicates that in character they would be strong willed and strong minded. In addition, they are politically astute. Allow me to illustrate what 1 mean.
This lesson of political astuteness was well learned when the party that now forms the minority government opposite and their national president came into the Cochrane riding to try to manipulate the political situation in such a way that it would serve their interests. The story is on record in the newspapers of the time. To put it very quickly and simply, the
situation which they tried to manipulate blew up in their faces. The imprint of egg on some Tory visages will be difficult to erase for a long time to come. It gives us something to laugh about and we certainly need that, especially when the winter months come with the chilly Arctic winds sweeping down upon our bushland and into our scattered towns and small villages. A good belly laugh at that time does a lot to help the circulation.
Incidentally, I should point out that some of our television viewers in northern Ontario are now able to enjoy, thanks to satellite communications, programs all the way from Atlanta, Georgia. Atlanta has come to have a special interest for us in the Cochrane riding. We understand that this place in the southern United States is now the heavenly emporium for forlorne floorwalkers who have stumbled and fallen in the service of nation and party.
During the course of this so-called throne speech debate members on this side of the House have used a variety of terms in seeking to describe the present Government of Canada accurately. Thus, we have heard reference to frittering, inexperience, naivete, and confusion. Many have spoken about the government's unsureness, uncertainty, and lack of clarity. Some have been so bold as to suggest that what we see opposite is vacillation and evasion, and that the throne speech is, to quote one member, without commitment to anything.
When I observe the actions of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Epp), a minister whose activities 1 will be following with considerable interest during the life of this Parliament as the critic for Northern Development, the word which springs into my mind is none of the ones I have already mentioned. Rather, the word that comes to my mind is ineptitude.
I, and others on this side of the House, regret very much that such a distinguished member as the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Holmes) was not given the portfolio of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. How long and how hard this man laboured in the opposition vineyard as the critic for this important area of responsibility! He gained much respect for his diligence and the degree of understanding which he acquired during those many years. Now what is his reward? His reward is to play no more than second fiddle to the maestro from Provencher who is the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
I want to talk about some of the activities of that minister, particularly in initiating, without coming to this House, some very significant constitutional changes in the Yukon territory. Perhaps with Your Honour's consent and the consent of all members 1 can begin that topic tomorrow, and now call it six o'clock.
